purpose: auditctl - a utility to assist controlling the kernel's audit system
sections:
[{"title":"SYNOPSIS","code":"auditctl [options]"},{"title":"DESCRIPTION","code":"The auditctl program configures kernel auditing options, displays
audit configuration status, and loads discretionary audit rules."},{"title":"CONFIGURATION OPTIONS","code":"-b backlog
    Sets the maximum number of outstanding audit buffers allowed
    (kernel default = 64). When all buffers are full, the kernel
    consults the failure flag for what to do.

--backlog_wait_time wait_time
    Sets the kernel wait time (kernel default 60*HZ) when the backlog
    limit is reached before queuing additional audit events. Must be
    >=0 and <10x the default value.

--reset_backlog_wait_time_actual
    Resets the actual backlog wait time counter shown by the status
    command.

-c
    Continue loading rules despite errors, summarizing results at the
    end. The exit code will not indicate success if any rule failed
    to load.

-D
    Delete all rules and watches. Can accept a key option (-k).

-e [0..2]
    Set the enabled flag: 0=temporarily disable auditing, 1=enable
    auditing, 2=lock the configuration (no further changes without a
    reboot). Locked mode audits and denies all further configuration
    change attempts.

-f [0..2]
    Set the failure mode: 0=silent, 1=printk, 2=panic. Determines how
    the kernel handles critical errors (transmission errors, backlog
    exceeded, out of memory, rate limit exceeded). Default is 1;
    secure environments typically use 2.

-h
    Display help information.

-i
    When used alone, ignore errors when reading rules from a file,
    always returning a success exit code. With -s, provide a
    human-readable interpretation of numbers.

--loginuid-immutable
    Instruct the kernel to make loginuids unchangeable once set.
    Requires CAP_AUDIT_CONTROL. Makes loginuid tamper-proof but may
    cause problems in certain containers.

-q mount-point,subtree
    For existing directory watches with bind or move mounts, tell the
    kernel to tag the mounted subtree for watching. Note the comma
    separator between values.

-r rate
    Set the message rate limit in messages/sec (0=none). Exceeding
    this rate consults the failure flag. Default is 0.

--reset-lost
    Reset the lost record counter shown by the status command.

-R file
    Read and execute auditctl commands from a file, line by line. The
    file must be owned by root and not readable by other users. Empty
    lines and lines starting with '#' are skipped.

--signal signal
    Send a signal to the audit daemon (requires privileges).
    Supported: TERM, HUP, USR1, USR2, CONT, and the user-friendly
    forms stop, reload, rotate, resume, state.

-t
    Trim subtrees after a mount command."},{"title":"STATUS OPTIONS","code":"-l
    List all rules, one per line. Can combine with -k (list rules
    matching a key) or -i (interpret syscall arguments).

-m text
    Send a user-space message into the audit system (requires
    CAP_AUDIT_WRITE, normally available to root). Creates a USER-type
    event.

-s
    Report kernel audit subsystem status: the in-kernel values
    configurable via -e, -f, -r, and -b, the audit daemon PID (0 =
    daemon not running), the lost event count, and the backlog queue
    size. Can be followed by -i for interpretation.

-v
    Print the auditctl version."},{"title":"RULE OPTIONS","code":"-a [list,action | action,list]
    Append a rule to the end of a list with an action. Fields may be
    in either order. Valid list names: task (per-task list, used only
    at fork/clone — only fields known at task-creation time apply),
    exit (syscall exit list — determines whether to create an audit
    event on syscall exit), user (user-space message filter list —
    valid fields: uid, auid, gid, pid, subj_user, subj_role,
    subj_type, subj_sen, subj_clr, msgtype, executable name), exclude
    (event-type exclusion filter, e.g. to drop avc messages),
    filesystem (applied to whole filesystems by fstype field),
    io_uring (io_uring syscall filter, using -S syscall notation).
    Valid actions: never (suppress event generation entirely), always
    (allocate audit context at entry, fill it in, write the record at
    exit).

-A list,action
    Add a rule to the beginning of a list with an action.

-C [f=f | f!=f]
    Build an inter-field comparison rule using equal/not-equal
    operators; multiple comparisons are supported. Valid fields: auid,
    uid, euid, suid, fsuid, obj_uid (one group); gid, egid, sgid,
    fsgid, obj_gid (another group) — groups cannot be mixed, but
    comparisons within a group are allowed.

-d list,action
    Delete a rule from a list with an action, only if it exactly
    matches the syscall name(s) and all field names/values.

-F [n=v | n!=v | n<v | n>v | n<=v | n>=v | n&v | n&=v]
    Build a rule field (up to 64 fields per command line), using one
    of 8 operators: equal, not equal, less than, greater than,
    less-or-equal, greater-or-equal, bit mask, bit test. User/group
    names are converted to numeric IDs. Valid fields include: a0-a3
    (first 4 syscall arguments, numeric only), arch (CPU architecture
    — use b32/b64 for the 32/64-bit syscall table; should precede -S),
    auid (original login UID), devmajor/devminor, dir (directory to
    watch recursively, exit list only), egid/euid, exe (absolute path
    to the executing binary, =/!= only, once per rule), exit (syscall
    exit value, errno text supported), fsgid/fsuid, fstype (debugfs/
    tracefs only, filesystem list), filetype (file, dir, socket, link,
    character, block, fifo), gid, inode, key (alternative to -k),
    msgtype (exclude/user lists), obj_uid/obj_gid, obj_user/obj_role/
    obj_type, obj_lev_low/obj_lev_high, path (file to watch, exit list
    only), perm (r/w/x/a file-operation filter, usable without -S),
    pers (OS personality number), pid/ppid, saddr_fam (address family
    number, IPv4=2/IPv6=10), sessionid, subj_user/subj_role/subj_type,
    subj_sen/subj_clr, sgid, success (yes if exit>=0; use 1 for true,
    0 for false), suid, uid.

-k key
    Set a filter key (arbitrary text, up to 31 bytes) that uniquely
    identifies audit records generated by a rule. Useful for grouping
    related rules; searchable via ausearch -k, usable with -D/-l to
    select rules. A rule can carry multiple keys.

-p [r|w|x|a]
    Describe the file-system watch trigger permissions: r=read,
    w=write, x=execute, a=attribute change (syscall-based, not
    standard file permission bits).

-S [syscall name or number | all]
    Specify a syscall by name, number, or 'all'. Multiple -S options
    (or a comma-separated list) improve performance over separate
    rules. On bi-arch systems (e.g. x86_64) rules apply to both 32-
    and 64-bit syscalls unless an arch directive says otherwise — the
    arch directive should precede -S.

-w path
    Insert a watch for a file-system object at path. Cannot watch a
    top-level directory; no wildcard support; tracked internally by
    inode. A file watch is equivalent to -F path=..., a directory
    watch to -F dir=.... Valid only with -p and -k. For finer-grained
    filtering (e.g. specific user access), use the full syscall-rule
    form with path/dir fields instead.

-W path
    Remove a watch for a file-system object at path — must match the
    original rule exactly."},{"title":"PERFORMANCE TIPS","code":"Syscall rules are evaluated on every syscall for every program, so
excessive rules degrade performance. Combine rules that share the same
filter, action, key, and fields — e.g. use multiple -S options in one
rule instead of separate rules for openat and truncate. Prefer
file-system auditing (-w / -F path=/dir=) where practical: the kernel
only evaluates it on filesystem-related syscalls rather than every
syscall."},{"title":"DISABLED BY DEFAULT","code":"Many systems ship a default -a never,task rule that causes new
processes to skip audit processing entirely, avoiding syscall-auditing
overhead. To enable auditing, remove 10-no-audit.rules and add
10-base-config.rules. Check auditctl -l to verify no never,task rule
conflicts with the rules you've defined."},{"title":"EXAMPLES","code":"# By pid
auditctl -a always,exit -S all -F pid=1005

# By executable path
auditctl -a always,exit -S all -F exe=/usr/bin/ls

# Files opened by a specific user (by auid)
auditctl -a always,exit -S openat -F auid=510

# Unsuccessful openat calls
auditctl -a always,exit -S openat -F success=0

# Watch a file for changes (two equivalent forms)
auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p wa
auditctl -a always,exit -F path=/etc/shadow -F perm=wa

# Recursively watch a directory
auditctl -w /etc/ -p wa
auditctl -a always,exit -F dir=/etc/ -F perm=wa

# Detect an admin accessing another user's files
auditctl -a always,exit -F dir=/home/ -F uid=0 -C auid!=obj_uid

# Example rules file
-D
-A exclude,always -F exe=/usr/bin/sudo"},{"title":"FILES","code":"/etc/audit/audit.rules
/etc/audit/audit-stop.rules"},{"title":"SEE ALSO","code":"audit.rules(7), ausearch(8), aureport(8), auditd(8)"}]

purpose: ausearch - a tool to query audit daemon logs
sections:
[{"title":"SYNOPSIS","code":"ausearch [options]"},{"title":"DESCRIPTION","code":"ausearch queries audit daemon logs based on different search criteria;
it also accepts raw log data from stdin. Command-line options are
combined as AND conditions (e.g. -m plus -ui returns events matching
both the given type and user ID) — the exception is -m and -n, which
accept multiple values that match on ANY of them.

Each syscall transition from user space to kernel and back generates
one unique event ID shared by every auditable record triggered during
that trip, for correlation. The kernel may add supplemental records to
an event — e.g. an open syscall's audit event also generates a PATH
record with the filename — so ausearch presents every record making up
one event together, meaning a search for a specific record type may
still return SYSCALL records alongside it. Not every record type
carries every field: PATH records, for instance, lack hostname or
loginuid."},{"title":"SEARCH OPTIONS","code":"-a, --event audit-event-id
    Search by event ID — the number after the colon in
    msg=audit(1116360555.329:2401771). All records from one syscall
    share an event ID; the next syscall gets a new one.

--arch CPU
    Search by CPU architecture. Use b32/b64 for the 32/64-bit syscall
    table; find your machine's arch with `uname -m`.

-c, --comm comm-name
    Search by the executable name recorded in the task structure.

-e, --exit exit-code-or-errno
    Search by syscall exit code or errno.

-f, --file file-name
    Search by filename (normal files and af_unix sockets).

-ga, --gid-all all-group-id / -ge, --gid-effective / -gi, --gid
    Search by group ID or name: -ga matches either the effective or
    real group ID; -ge matches the effective group ID specifically;
    -gi matches the (real) group ID.

-hn, --host host-name
    Search by hostname, FQDN, or numeric address (no resolution is
    performed) — corresponds to the addr/host field. See --node for
    the separate node field.

-i, --interpret
    Convert numeric entities to text (e.g. uid to account name). On
    unenriched logs this uses the current machine's resources, so a
    renamed account can be misleading; enriched logs carry the mapping
    and are portable across machines.

-k, --key key-string
    Search by the audit rule's key string.

-m, --message message-type[,message-type,...]
    Search by message (record) type — comma-separated list or repeated
    -m options. ALL retrieves every message type (it isn't a real type
    itself). Run with no argument to print the valid type list.

-o, --object SE-Linux-context-string
    Search where the object (tcontext) matches the given string.

-p, --pid process-id / -pp, --ppid parent-process-id
    Search by process ID or parent process ID.

-sc, --syscall syscall-name-or-value
    Search by syscall, by name (per your machine's syscall table) or
    numeric value.

-se, --context / -su, --subject / -o, --object SE-Linux-context-string
    -se matches either scontext (subject) or tcontext (object); -su
    matches scontext (subject) only.

--session Login-Session-ID
    Search by the login session ID assigned at login and carried by
    every descendant process.

-sv, --success yes|no
    Search by success value.

-te, --end / -ts, --start [date] [time]
    Search by an end/start timestamp. Format follows locale (check
    with `date +%x`); an omitted date assumes today, an omitted time
    assumes midnight (-ts) or now (-te); 24-hour clock. Keywords: now,
    recent (10 minutes ago), this-hour, boot, today, yesterday,
    this-week, week-ago, this-month, this-year, and (for -ts only)
    checkpoint (recover from a valid checkpoint file's timestamp,
    ignoring its recorded inode/device/serial/node/type — for use
    after ausearch exits 10/11/12).

-tm, --terminal terminal
    Search by terminal value (daemons like cron/atd use their daemon
    name as the terminal).

-ua, --uid-all / -ue, --uid-effective / -ui, --uid / -ul, --loginuid
    Search by user ID: -ua matches uid, euid, OR auid; -ue matches the
    effective UID; -ui matches the (real) UID; -ul matches the login
    UID (auid) specifically — requires the program's entry point to be
    PAMified with pam_loginuid for an accurate auid.

-uu, --uuid guest-uuid / -vm, --vm-name guest-name
    Search by guest VM UUID or name.

-w, --word
    Require whole-word matches for filename, hostname, terminal, keys,
    and SE Linux context searches.

-x, --executable executable
    Search by executable name."},{"title":"OUTPUT & CONTROL OPTIONS","code":"--checkpoint checkpoint-file
    Checkpoint output between successive ausearch invocations so only
    new events print on the next run. Loads the prior checkpoint,
    discards already-seen complete events until it matches the
    checkpointed one, then prints new ones. Errors out if the file or
    the checkpointed event can't be found.

--eoe-timeout seconds
    Override the end-of-event parsing timeout (see
    end_of_event_timeout in auditd.conf(5)) for this run.

--escape raw|tty|shell|shell_quote
    Control output escaping; each mode includes the prior mode's
    escaped characters plus more. tty is the default.

--extra-keys / --extra-labels / --extra-obj2 / --extra-time
    In --format csv mode, add extra columns: rule key info from
    SYSCALL records (--extra-keys), subject/object SE Linux labels
    (--extra-labels), second-object info for renames/mounts
    (--extra-obj2), or broken-down time fields (--extra-time).

--format raw|default|interpret|csv|text
    raw = unformatted; default = a visual separator + timestamp then
    the event's records; interpret = numeric entities converted to
    text; csv = normalized comma-separated values for analysis tools;
    text = converted to readable English sentences.

-if, --input file-name|directory / --input-logs
    Read from a specific file/directory instead of the default logs
    (path capped at 4064 bytes), or from the log location configured
    in auditd.conf (needed when running ausearch from cron).

--just-one
    Stop after the first matching event.

-l, --line-buffered
    Flush output on every line — useful when stdout is a pipe where
    the default block buffering is undesirable (at some performance
    cost).

-n, --node
    Search by node field (multiple nodes allowed; any match counts).
    See -hn/--host for the separate host field.

-r, --raw
    Output completely unformatted data — useful for extracting records
    to feed to another audit tool.

-v, --version
    Print version and exit.

-h, --help
    Display help.

--debug
    Write malformed, skipped events to stderr."},{"title":"EXIT STATUS","code":"0   OK
1   nothing found, argument errors, or minor file access/read errors
10  invalid checkpoint data found in the checkpoint file
11  checkpoint processing error
12  checkpointed event not found in the matching log file"},{"title":"NOTE","code":"The boot time keyword has a limitation: it's computed as "time now
minus /proc/uptime", so a post-boot clock adjustment (e.g. via ntp)
can throw it off — specify the time fully in that case. Check the
calculated boot time with:
date -d "$(cut -f1 -d. /proc/uptime) seconds ago""},{"title":"EXAMPLES","code":"# Search for a specific user
ausearch --start today --loginuid john -i

# Check today's SELinux denials
ausearch --start today -m avc -i

# Output in readable-sentence form
ausearch --start today --format text

# TTY keystroke events, interpreted and shell-escaped
ausearch --start today -m TTY -i --escape shell_quote"},{"title":"SEE ALSO","code":"auditd(8), auditd.conf(5), aureport(8), pam_loginuid(8)"}]

purpose: aureport - a tool that produces summary reports of audit daemon logs
sections:
[{"title":"SYNOPSIS","code":"aureport [options]"},{"title":"DESCRIPTION","code":"aureport produces summary reports of the audit system logs (it also
accepts raw log data via stdin). Reports include column labels for
field interpretation. Except for the main summary report, every report
shows the audit event number, so a specific hit can be looked up in
full with `ausearch -a`. aureport's output is meant as a building
block for more complex analysis, not a final answer by itself."},{"title":"REPORT SELECTION OPTIONS","code":"-au, --auth        Report on authentication attempts
-a, --avc          Report on AVC (SELinux/AppArmor) messages
--comm             Report on commands run
-c, --config       Report on config changes
-cr, --crypto      Report on crypto events
-e, --event        Report on events
-f, --file         Report on files and af_unix sockets
-h, --host         Report on hosts
--integrity        Report on integrity events
-k, --key          Report on audit rule keys
-l, --login        Report on logins
-m, --mods         Report on account modifications
-ma, --mac         Report on Mandatory Access Control events
-n, --anomaly      Report on anomaly events (e.g. NIC promiscuous
                   mode, program segfaults)
-p, --pid          Report on processes
-r, --response     Report on responses to anomaly events
-s, --syscall      Report on syscalls
--summary          Run a summary report, totaling the main report's
                   elements
-t, --log          Output the start/end time of each log
--tty              Report on TTY keystrokes
-tm, --terminal    Report on terminals
-u, --user         Report on users
--virt             Report on virtualization events
-x, --executable   Report on executables"},{"title":"FILTER & OUTPUT OPTIONS","code":"--failed / --success
    Select only failed or only successful events (default is both).

-i, --interpret
    Interpret numeric entities into text (e.g. uid to account name).

-if, --input file|directory / --input-logs
    Use the given file/directory instead of the default logs (path
    capped at 4064 bytes), or the log location configured in
    auditd.conf (needed for running aureport from cron).

--node node-name
    Select events from the given node; multiple nodes allowed.

-nc, --no-config
    Exclude CONFIG_CHANGE events — useful for a key report when audit
    rules themselves carry labels.

-te, --end / -ts, --start [date] [time]
    Select events before/after the given time — same locale-dependent
    formats and keywords (now, recent, this-hour, boot, today,
    yesterday, this-week, week-ago, this-month, this-year) as
    ausearch's -te/-ts.

--escape raw|tty|shell|shell_quote
    Control output escaping, same modes as ausearch.

--eoe-timeout seconds
    Override the end-of-event parsing timeout for this run.

--debug
    Write malformed, skipped events to stderr.

-v, --version / --help
    Print version and exit / print a brief command summary."},{"title":"NOTE","code":"Boot-time calculation uses current time minus /proc/uptime and can be
thrown off by a post-boot NTP adjustment. Verify with:
date -d "$(cut -f1 -d. /proc/uptime) seconds ago""},{"title":"SEE ALSO","code":"ausearch(8), auditd(8), auditd.conf(5)"}]

[{"title":"SYNOPSIS","code":"auditd [-f] [-l] [-n] [-s disable|enable|nochange] [-c <config_dir>]"},{"title":"DESCRIPTION","code":"auditd is the userspace component of the Linux Auditing System; it's
responsible for writing audit records to disk. Logs are read with
ausearch or aureport; system configuration and rule loading go through
auditctl. At startup, rules from /etc/audit/audit.rules are loaded via
auditctl; augenrules offers an alternative path, reading rules from
/etc/audit/rules.d/ and compiling them into that same file. The
daemon's own configuration lives in auditd.conf."},{"title":"OPTIONS","code":"-f
    Leave the audit daemon in the foreground for debugging; messages
    also go to stderr rather than only the audit log.

-l
    Allow the audit daemon to follow symlinks for config files.

-n
    No fork — useful when run from inittab or systemd.

-s ENABLE_STATE
    Specify whether auditd should change the kernel's enabled flag at
    startup: disable, enable, or nochange (default enables it). The
    same flag can be changed at runtime with auditctl -e.

-c
    Specify an alternate config file directory (default
    /etc/audit/); this directory is also passed to the dispatcher."},{"title":"SIGNALS","code":"SIGHUP    Reread the configuration file and apply changes if it's
          syntactically valid.
SIGTERM   Stop event processing, write a shutdown event, and exit.
SIGUSR1   Immediately rotate the logs.
SIGUSR2   Attempt to resume logging and passing events to plugins.
SIGCONT   Dump a report of internal state to /var/run/auditd.state."},{"title":"EXIT CODES","code":"1   Initialization failure (priority adjustment, daemonization, audit
    netlink access, etc.)
2   Invalid command-line arguments
4   Insufficient daemon privileges
6   Configuration file error"},{"title":"FILES","code":"/etc/audit/auditd.conf   daemon configuration
/etc/audit/audit.rules   startup rules
/etc/audit/rules.d/      individual rule sets
/etc/audit/plugins.d/    plugin configurations
/etc/audit/audit-stop    shutdown rules
/var/run/auditd.state    internal state report"},{"title":"SEE ALSO","code":"auditd.conf(5), auditd-plugins(5), ausearch(8), aureport(8), auditctl(8),
augenrules(8), audit.rules(7)"}]

purpose: augenrules - a script that merges component audit rule files
sections:
[{"title":"SYNOPSIS","code":"augenrules [--check] [--load]"},{"title":"DESCRIPTION","code":"augenrules consolidates the audit rule files in /etc/audit/rules.d/
into a single /etc/audit/audit.rules file. Only files ending in
".rules" are processed; everything else in that directory is ignored.

Files are concatenated in natural sort order, with empty lines and
comments stripped. A few directives get special placement regardless
of source-file order: a final bare -D appears first, -b directives
second, -f directives third, and -e directives last in the merged
output. /etc/audit/audit.rules is only rewritten when the merged
result actually differs from what's already there."},{"title":"OPTIONS","code":"--check
    Test whether the rules have changed and would need updating,
    without actually overwriting audit.rules.

--load
    Load the old (or newly built) rules into the kernel."},{"title":"FILES","code":"/etc/audit/rules.d/
/etc/audit/audit.rules"},{"title":"SEE ALSO","code":"audit.rules(7), auditctl(8), auditd(8)"}]

purpose: autrace - a program similar to strace, built on the audit subsystem
sections:
[{"title":"SYNOPSIS","code":"autrace program [-r] [program-args]..."},{"title":"DESCRIPTION","code":"autrace traces a single process's execution the way strace does, but
using audit rules rather than ptrace: it executes the given program
(passing along any arguments) and directs the resulting audit data to
the audit logs (if auditd is running) or to syslog. It automatically
removes all audit rules both before and after running the program — as
a safeguard, it requires that every existing rule already be deleted
via auditctl before it will proceed."},{"title":"OPTIONS","code":"-r
    Limit the syscalls collected to just those needed for analyzing
    resource usage. Useful for threat modeling; keeps the resulting
    log smaller."},{"title":"EXAMPLES","code":"# Standard usage
autrace /bin/ls /tmp
ausearch --start recent -p 2442 -i

# Resource-usage mode
autrace -r /bin/ls
ausearch --start recent -p 2450 --raw | aureport --file --summary
ausearch --start recent -p 2450 --raw | aureport --host --summary"},{"title":"SEE ALSO","code":"ausearch(8), auditctl(8)"}]

purpose: event multiplexor — merged into auditd itself as of audit 3.0
sections:
[{"title":"STATUS","code":"audispd no longer has a standalone man page on current systems (RHEL 9/
Ubuntu 22.04+ ship audit >= 3.0). In audit 3.0, the audispd dispatcher
daemon's code was merged directly into auditd, and audispd.conf's
settings moved into auditd.conf. The dispatcher and disp_qos options in
auditd.conf were deprecated as part of that same merge. What was
/etc/audisp/plugins.d/ is now /etc/audit/plugins.d/, documented by the
current auditd-plugins(5) man page below rather than a separate
audispd(8) — the fetch for a live audispd(8) page 404s on both current
Ubuntu manpages releases checked (jammy, noble) for exactly this
reason, which is real signal, not a gap in this transcription."},{"title":"auditd-plugins(5) — the modern replacement","code":"NAME
    auditd-plugins — realtime event receivers

DESCRIPTION
    auditd can multiplex audit events in real time, distributing them
    to child programs for real-time analysis. Plugin configuration
    files live in /etc/audit/plugins.d (configurable via plugin_dir in
    auditd.conf). auditd scans that directory at startup, starts every
    active plugin, and restarts failed ones up to max_restarts times.

PLUGIN CONFIGURATION OPTIONS
    active     yes or no
    direction  in or out (inbound is not yet supported)
    path       absolute path to the plugin executable (or a name, for
               internal plugins)
    type       currently only "builtin" is supported
    args       arguments passed to the child program (max 2)
    format     binary or string (default string) — how events are
               formatted for the plugin

FILES
    /etc/audit/auditd.conf
    /etc/audit/plugins.d

SEE ALSO
    auditd.conf(5), auditd(8), execve(2), auparse_feed(3)"}]
